Activation steering works by adding a direction in residual stream space — computed as the mean difference between paired activations — to shift model behavior toward a target concept at inference time. The central question here is whether you can compose multiple such vectors (e.g., "French" + "angry" + "formal") additively and get the intended joint behavior, or whether semantic conflict between concepts causes the intervention to degrade, collapse to one dominant concept, or produce incoherent outputs. The key concepts are: linearity assumptions in superposition (the model encodes features as approximately linear directions), interference when those directions are not orthogonal, and the distinction between syntactic composition (vectors that modify style or register) versus semantic composition (vectors with conflicting propositional content, like "truthful" + "deceptive"). What a beginner misses is that the residual stream isn't a neutral summation buffer — downstream attention heads and MLPs apply nonlinear transformations that can amplify small angular conflicts into catastrophic behavioral interference, so a pair of vectors that each work beautifully in isolation can destructively interact not because the concepts are logically contradictory, but because they activate overlapping circuits that compete for the same downstream computational resources. An expert also worries specifically about asymmetric dominance: one vector consistently wins not due to semantic priority but due to norm magnitude or layer placement, which means naive composition silently fails without any obvious output signal that something went wrong.

If two vectors causally route through the same attention heads, the prediction is interference rather than independence: those heads are being asked to simultaneously implement two different query/key/value transformations, and since attention patterns are determined by softmax over a single set of logits, the composed input will produce a pattern that satisfies neither intervention cleanly — you'd expect behavioral output that's a distorted blend, or dominance by whichever vector shifts the head's input distribution more dramatically. This is directly testable via causal mediation analysis (as formalized in Meng et al.'s ROME work and the broader path patching framework from Wang et al.'s IOI paper): patch each steering vector independently through specific heads, measure the indirect effect on the output metric, then compare the sum of individual indirect effects to the indirect effect under joint composition — a superadditivity or subadditivity gap there localizes the interference. Concretely, in the Indirect Object Identification circuit in GPT-2, a small set of heads (the S-inhibition heads, particularly heads 8.6, 9.9, 10.0) dominate name suppression; two vectors that both have high indirect effect through those heads would be predicted to interfere badly, while vectors whose causal mass falls on disjoint head sets should compose more cleanly. A quantitative threshold that matters: Conmy et al.'s ACDC work suggests that in many GPT-2 circuits, 3–5 heads account for >80% of a behavior's causal effect, so "overlap" is a small-integer problem, not a diffuse one. The confound experts worry about here is that two vectors might use different heads but write to the same residual stream subspace at the same layer, producing interference downstream that head-level analysis alone would miss — so you need both head-level path patching and subspace projection analysis (e.g., checking cosine similarity of the vectors' projections into each layer's dominant singular directions) to fully characterize the interaction.

The clean diagnostic is to norm-equalize both vectors before composition — rescale each to unit L2 norm (or to a shared fixed norm matching your typical steering magnitude) and rerun the intervention; if dominance persists after equalization, norm was not the cause, and you're looking at geometric alignment with the model's activation distribution. To test the alignment hypothesis specifically, project both vectors onto the top principal components of the residual stream at the intervention layer, computed from a large sample of clean forward passes — if the dominant vector has substantially higher explained variance in that PCA basis (say, >2× the projection magnitude of the subordinate vector onto the top 10–20 PCs), that's evidence it's riding high-variance directions the model already uses heavily. This distinction matters because the mechanisms have different implications: norm dominance is an artifact of how you constructed the vectors (e.g., one was computed from a larger or more homogeneous contrast set), while alignment dominance reflects something real about the model's representational geometry — specifically, that certain behavioral dimensions are encoded along directions that also carry high natural variance, making them more "load-bearing" for downstream computation. Anthropic's linear representation probing work and the representation engineering results from Zou et al. (2023) both implicitly touch this: their contrast-pair vectors for concepts like "honesty" tend to align with high-variance directions, which is part of why they're effective but also why they can swamp other simultaneous interventions. A further refinement is to measure each vector's alignment with the effective subspace — not raw PCA but the directions that most influence the specific output you're measuring, recoverable via gradient-weighted activation analysis — because a vector can sit in a high-variance direction that is nevertheless causally inert for your target behavior, and conflating variance with causal relevance is the central error beginners make here.

Yes, the implication holds with an important asymmetry: concepts encoded along low-variance directions require larger intervention magnitudes to produce behavioral change, because downstream MLP and attention computations are effectively calibrated to treat those directions as noise — the model's weights have high sensitivity to perturbations along high-variance axes and low sensitivity along low-variance ones, which is exactly what PCA variance structure reflects about the Hessian of the loss with respect to activations. This predicts that "rare" or "suppressed" behaviors — think: a language model producing outputs in a style it almost never generates, or exhibiting a personality trait underrepresented in training — will require steering vectors with much larger norms to achieve equivalent behavioral shift, pushing you into a regime where the intervention itself distorts the broader distribution, producing incoherence artifacts unrelated to the target concept. There's a further prediction about compositional steerability: when you compose a high-variance vector with a low-variance one, the low-variance concept will be dominated not just because of norm differences but because the model's nonlinearities systematically amplify perturbations in high-variance directions — so you'd expect a consistent asymmetry where common behaviors hijack multi-concept interventions involving rare behaviors, regardless of how carefully you equalize norms. The uncomfortable implication for alignment is that behaviors a model has been trained to suppress (e.g., via RLHF) may be encoded in precisely these low-variance, hard-to-steer directions — not because suppression was explicitly designed that way, but because reinforcement fine-tuning reduces the variance of suppressed-behavior activations, making them geometrically harder to reactivate via linear intervention, which is one reason activation steering jailbreaks require much larger multipliers than prosocial steering interventions.

Steering resistance as a suppression audit is a genuinely promising idea, but it requires disentangling two confounds: a behavior can be hard to steer toward either because it was actively suppressed during fine-tuning or because it was simply rare in pretraining and therefore never developed a strong linear representation in the first place — and these two histories produce identical geometric signatures (low-variance, high steering threshold) but have completely different interpretive significance. The cleanest way to separate them is to compare steering resistance in the base model versus the fine-tuned model for the same behavior: if resistance is high in both, it's a pretraining rarity artifact; if resistance increases specifically post-fine-tuning, that delta is your suppression signal, and its magnitude gives you a rough proxy for suppression intensity. Mechanistically, this works because RLHF reduces the probability of suppressed outputs, which over many gradient steps shrinks the activations associated with those behaviors toward the mean of the safe-output distribution — measurable as a reduction in the norm of the contrast-pair vector and increased entanglement with irrelevant high-variance directions. There's preliminary empirical support in the "refusal direction" literature: Arditi et al. (2024) on refusal ablation in Llama and Claude-family models found that refusal behavior is concentrated in a surprisingly low-dimensional subspace, and that this subspace is more compressed in more heavily fine-tuned models, consistent with the prediction that fine-tuning progressively collapses suppressed-behavior variance. The audit use case is real but has a critical limitation: behaviors that were suppressed early and thoroughly may have their representations actively overwritten rather than merely compressed — in which case steering resistance goes to infinity not because of geometric suppression but because the representational scaffold for the behavior no longer exists in recoverable form, and you'd misread absence of steerability as maximal suppression rather than as erasure.

Compression versus erasure do have distinguishable signatures, and the most direct one is whether a linear probe trained on base-model activations transfers to the fine-tuned model: if the concept is compressed, a probe trained on the base model will still decode above chance from fine-tuned activations (the direction exists but has small variance), whereas if it's erased, transfer probe accuracy drops to chance, indicating the representational direction has been rotated or overwritten by fine-tuning gradient steps. A second signature lives in the MLP weights directly: compressed behaviors should still activate sparse features in the MLP layers associated with that concept (detectable via dictionary learning / sparse autoencoders as in Bricken et al.'s one-layer transformer work and Cunningham et al. 2023 on residual stream SAEs), while erased behaviors would show dropout of the relevant SAE features entirely in the fine-tuned model — this is now practically testable given that Anthropic has published SAE feature sets for Claude Sonnet 3 at multiple layers. The distinction matters enormously for recovery: compressed representations are recoverable via activation steering, fine-tuning on small contrastive datasets, or even inference-time prompt engineering that reactivates the dormant direction, whereas erased representations require retraining from a checkpoint predating the erasure, since the information is no longer present in the weights in any linearly accessible form. A subtler third signature is the loss landscape around the suppressed behavior: compression leaves a shallow valley in the loss surface that few-shot fine-tuning can quickly re-enter (explaining why RLHF models can be "unlocked" with small LoRA interventions — sometimes as few as 100–200 examples as shown in Yang et al. 2023 on refusal bypasses), while erasure produces a flat region where gradient signal for recovery is genuinely absent. The practical alignment implication is that compression-only suppression is a much weaker safety guarantee than it appears — the behavior is latent and recoverable by any party with fine-tuning access — whereas genuine erasure, if achievable, would be a stronger guarantee, but current evidence from probing and SAE analysis suggests most RLHF suppression produces compression rather than erasure, meaning the representations survive fine-tuning in recoverable form.

Persistent SAE features with reduced activation frequency is strong evidence for gating-level suppression, and the mechanism is likely implemented in the bias terms and early MLP layers that control feature activation thresholds — RLHF gradient updates would preferentially shift the pre-activation inputs to suppressed features below their ReLU/SoLU firing threshold across the training distribution, without needing to rotate or destroy the feature direction itself, which is geometrically cheaper and explains why compression is the typical outcome. The critical prediction about distributional shift is that gating-level suppression is inherently fragile: the suppression is calibrated to the training distribution of prompts seen during RLHF, and out-of-distribution inputs — unusual syntax, non-English text, domain-shifted contexts, or adversarially crafted prefixes — can shift the pre-activation values enough to push suppressed features back above threshold, reactivating the behavior without any explicit jailbreak mechanism. This fragility is empirically visible in the multilingual jailbreak literature: Yong et al. (2023) showed that Claude and GPT-4 exhibit significantly higher rates of harmful completions in low-resource languages, which is exactly what gating-level suppression predicts — the RLHF gate was trained predominantly on English prompts, so the gate doesn't close reliably when the residual stream distribution shifts under non-English input. Representation-level suppression, by contrast, would be more robust to distributional shift because the feature direction itself has been altered — out-of-distribution inputs can't easily reactivate something that no longer has a coherent direction to activate along — but as argued above, this appears to be the rarer outcome of fine-tuning. The deeper mechanistic worry is that gating-level suppression may actually be implemented across multiple layers in a redundant cascade, meaning robustness comes not from any single strong gate but from the probability that all gates fail simultaneously under distributional shift — and adversarial inputs that shift the residual stream distribution monotonically across layers (which structured jailbreaks may do) could systematically open the entire cascade, explaining why complex multi-turn jailbreaks are more effective than single-shot ones.

The two regimes make distinct predictions about the layer-wise distribution of suppression signal: deepening adds new gate layers (the causal suppression effect, measured via path patching, spreads to layers that previously had near-zero indirect effect on the suppressed behavior), while strengthening concentrates the effect in the same layers but with larger magnitude — so the measurement is a layer-resolved causal mediation profile computed before and after additional RLHF, looking for whether the support of the indirect effect distribution widens or whether it narrows and intensifies. Empirically, the limited evidence available suggests strengthening dominates early in RLHF training while deepening emerges with extended training: this is consistent with findings from Anthropic's Constitutional AI work where iterative RLHF rounds progressively engaged earlier layers in refusal behavior, suggesting that prolonged training does recruit additional circuit depth rather than just amplifying existing gates. The practical measurement protocol would be: run ACDC or activation patching on the suppressed behavior at RLHF checkpoints N, 2N, 3N steps, extract the set of heads/MLPs with indirect effect above some threshold (say 10% of total effect), and track whether that set grows (deepening) or stays fixed with growing per-node effect magnitudes (strengthening) — this is feasible on open models like Llama-3 where intermediate fine-tuning checkpoints can be saved. Deepening has a critically different robustness implication: a deeper cascade is harder to bypass via single-layer activation steering or single-point jailbreaks, but it also means suppression has colonized more of the model's general computation, potentially degrading performance on legitimate tasks that share circuit components with the suppressed behavior — a cost that strengthening-only suppression would incur less severely. The regime distinction also predicts different LoRA recovery curves: if suppression is deep, a LoRA adapter targeting only late layers will fail to recover suppressed behavior even with many examples, while if suppression is shallow and strong, a late-layer LoRA will recover the behavior quickly — so the layer-restriction experiment on fine-tuning recovery gives you a second independent measurement of which regime you're in without requiring access to intermediate checkpoints.
